questions.prompt: How does adding dilute strong acid generally affect Mg(OH)2 solubility at fixed temperature if complex formation is negligible?
options: It increases solubility by consuming OH− from the dissolution equilibrium.
It decreases solubility because H3O+ is a common ion of Mg(OH)2
It increases Ksp directly
It has no effect because all solids ignore solution pH
questions.explanation: A is correct. Hydronium neutralizes hydroxide, favoring further dissolution to replenish a product. B is incorrect: hydronium is not a constituent ion of the hydroxide solid. C is incorrect: acid changes solution composition, not the fixed-temperature constant. D is incorrect: salts containing hydroxide can be strongly pH-sensitive.

questions.prompt: Why can a carbonate solid dissolve more readily in acid than in neutral water?
options: Acid supplies extra free carbonate
Protonation necessarily makes Ksp zero
Carbonate is protonated, reducing free CO3^2− and favoring dissolution.
The solid becomes electrically charged as a whole and disappears without products
questions.explanation: C is correct. Acid-base consumption of a constituent anion pulls the dissolution equilibrium forward; further carbonic-acid chemistry can reinforce this. A is incorrect: it consumes carbonate by protonation. B is incorrect: Ksp is unchanged at fixed temperature. D is incorrect: dissolution and proton transfer conserve atoms and charge.

questions.prompt: CaF2 is placed in dilute acid. HF is a weak acid, and no metal complexes form. What qualitative effect is expected?
options: Less dissolution because HF supplies a large common-ion fluoride concentration regardless of pH
No pH effect because fluorine is a nonmetal
All Ca2+ is reduced to calcium metal
Greater dissolution because F− is converted partly into HF.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Removing free fluoride through protonation allows more CaF2 to dissolve. A is incorrect: protonation lowers free F− rather than supplying it as assumed. B is incorrect: the anion acid-base equilibrium, not element classification, matters. C is incorrect: acid-base solubility changes do not imply metal reduction.

questions.prompt: AgCl is exposed to dilute HNO3 at fixed temperature. Assume no complexes, activity corrections, or side reactions; Cl− is not appreciably protonated. What pH-specific effect is expected?
options: A large increase because every anion is readily protonated in water
Little direct enhancement of dissolution from protonating chloride.
A decrease because HNO3 adds common Cl−
Ksp must increase in exact proportion to acidity
questions.explanation: B is correct. Chloride is the very weak conjugate base of a strong acid, so acid does not substantially remove it as molecular HCl in this model. A is incorrect: conjugate-base strength matters. C is incorrect: nitric acid supplies nitrate, not chloride. D is incorrect: composition does not change Ksp at fixed temperature.

questions.prompt: At constant temperature, OH− is added to a saturated Mg(OH)2 solution while complexation remains negligible. What happens to its molar solubility?
options: It increases because all high-pH solutions dissolve hydroxides
It remains unchanged because OH− is absent from Ksp
It decreases because added hydroxide is a common ion.
Ksp decreases because hydroxide was added
questions.explanation: C is correct. Higher free OH− favors solid formation until the ion product again matches Ksp. A is incorrect: hydroxide common-ion suppression applies here. B is incorrect: OH− appears squared in the expression. D is incorrect: the constant is unchanged at fixed temperature.

questions.prompt: A salt contains an anion that is a weak base. Its solutions are held separately at lower and higher pH, without metal complexation. Why may lower pH increase total dissolved salt?
options: More anion is protonated, reducing the free anion that enters Ksp.
Lower pH always makes every ion concentration individually smaller
The salt changes its stoichiometric formula in the Ksp expression
The equilibrium constant must become negative
questions.explanation: A is correct. Coupling to proton transfer allows greater total dissolution even though the free-ion product remains constrained. B is incorrect: more metal can dissolve while free anion is consumed. C is incorrect: the original dissolution equation remains the reference. D is incorrect: equilibrium constants remain positive.

questions.prompt: A metal hydroxide dissolves further after acidification at unchanged temperature. Which statement about its Ksp is correct?
options: Ksp must increase because more total metal dissolves
Ksp remains the same; free-ion concentrations redistribute.
Ksp must decrease because acid was consumed
Ksp no longer applies whenever any acid is present
questions.explanation: B is correct. Acid consumes hydroxide, and more solid dissolves while equilibrium still satisfies the same constant. A is incorrect: solubility and Ksp are not interchangeable when other equilibria change. C is incorrect: consuming acid does not alter the temperature-specific constant. D is incorrect: the dissolution equilibrium still constrains free ions under the stated model.

questions.prompt: Which constituent makes a salt especially likely to show acid-enhanced solubility through anion protonation?
options: An anion that is an extremely weak proton acceptor under the conditions
An inert neutral solid contaminant with no ions
A cation that is stipulated to have no acid-base or complexation behavior, paired with an inert anion
An anion that is an appreciable weak base in water.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Protonation removes free basic anion from the dissolution equilibrium. A is incorrect: such an anion is less readily removed by acid. B is incorrect: it does not provide the specified acid-base coupling. C is incorrect: no relevant pH-coupled process is supplied.

questions.prompt: An aqueous Mg2+ solution is made more basic. Over the range considered, soluble hydroxo complexes are negligible. Why can Mg(OH)2 precipitate?
options: OH− removes all Mg atoms by evaporation
Increasing OH− raises the ion product until it can exceed Ksp.
Higher pH forces Ksp to zero
Precipitation requires the solution to contain no water
questions.explanation: B is correct. Once the free-ion product is too large, solid formation reduces dissolved concentrations toward saturation. A is incorrect: that is not the precipitation mechanism. C is incorrect: the fixed-temperature Ksp remains unchanged. D is incorrect: the solid can form directly from an aqueous mixture.

questions.prompt: Compare adding a small amount of HCl or MgCl2 to saturated Mg(OH)2 at fixed temperature and negligible volume change. No complexes form. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both are equivalent because both contain chloride
Both raise Ksp because dissolved salt concentration increases
HCl favors dissolution by consuming OH−; MgCl2 suppresses it by supplying common Mg2+.
HCl supplies common hydroxide while MgCl2 neutralizes it
questions.explanation: C is correct. The two additions affect different free-ion concentrations in opposite directions. A is incorrect: chloride is a spectator here; hydronium and magnesium differ. B is incorrect: neither addition changes Ksp at fixed temperature. D is incorrect: the roles of the added species are reversed.

questions.prompt: A student acidifies AgCl suspensions using HCl and HNO3, then attributes different dissolved Ag+ amounts solely to pH. Assume dilute no-complexation conditions. What important difference must be controlled?
options: HCl also supplies common Cl−, which can suppress AgCl dissolution independently of pH.
HNO3 supplies common Ag+
Both acids necessarily change Ksp differently at the same temperature
No control is needed because all strong acids add identical ions
questions.explanation: A is correct. Acid identity changes ion composition as well as pH; chloride is not removed appreciably by protonation in this model. B is incorrect: nitric acid does not contain silver. C is incorrect: Ksp is a property of the specified dissolution equilibrium at that temperature. D is incorrect: their conjugate anions differ.
